title: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice

sections.title: Economic Systems and How Choices are Made

slides.title: Choices All Around Us
slides.kicker: Pocket money, libraries, farms: economics everywhere
bullets: Spend pocket money on snacks or save for shoes? A library with five copies but twenty students? These are economic choices.
Individuals, enterprises and governments all make economic choices, like a farmer picking crops or a nation picking highways or hospitals.
Every choice exists because resources like money, land and time are not endless.

left.title: You and your school
items: Who reads the five storybook copies first

right.title: Farm, factory, government
items: Which crop suits soil and rain
More labour or capital? Highways or hospitals

slides.note: Notice three choices you made before lunch today.

slides.title: Needs Versus Wants
slides.kicker: Food and shelter first, or the new gadget?
bullets: Needs are essentials like food, water and shelter. We cannot run daily life without them.
Wants are extras like gadgets, vacations or luxury items. They add comfort but are not essential.
Some of our preferences are needs and others are wants, so every spending decision starts with this sorting.
slides.note: Book activity: list three things your parents bought this month and sort them.

slides.title: Wants Keep Changing
slides.kicker: Bicycle today, motorbike tomorrow, car next?
bullets: Human wants are unlimited. They never stay satisfied for long and keep changing with time.
The book's example: people may want to upgrade from a bicycle to a motorbike and then to a car.
Unlimited, changing wants collide with limited resources, and that clash creates the problem of choice.
slides.note: Book asks: can too many wants create problems? Discuss with a friend.

slides.title: What Are Resources?
slides.kicker: From river water to factory technology
bullets: Resources are the factors used for the production of goods and services.
Natural resources come from nature, like water and coal.
Human-made resources are created by people, like capital and technology.
slides.note: Grade 8 flashback: these connect to the factors of production.

slides.title: One Resource, Many Uses
slides.kicker: Same steel, three very different futures
bullets: The book shows steel being used for medical equipment, aircraft manufacturing and refrigerator manufacturing.
Resources have alternative uses, so using steel for one product means other products get less of it.
This is why choosing among alternatives is unavoidable for households, enterprises and governments.
slides.note: Ek resource, kitne uses! That is scarcity in action.

slides.title: Markets: Physical and Virtual
slides.kicker: Where buying and selling actually happens
bullets: A market is a place where buying and selling of products and services takes place.
It could be a physical market you walk into, or a virtual one on the internet.
Markets connect buyers and sellers, so they matter for every economic choice we study.
slides.note: Your online shopping cart is a market too.

slides.title: Four Factors of Production
slides.kicker: Land, labour, capital and technology team up
bullets: In Grade 8 you met the factors of production: land, labour, capital and technology.
These factors are used for the production of goods and services that people need and want.
Each factor is limited, so producers must plan carefully how to combine them.
slides.note: Four ingredients, endless dishes: production in a nutshell.

slides.title: Resources Are Limited
slides.kicker: Scarce for families, scarce for nations
bullets: Both natural and human-made resources are limited in quantity, yet each has many alternative uses.
A household allocates money to buy fruit or a pair of shoes; the same rupees cannot buy both.
Economies also must use scarce resources in the best possible way to meet unlimited wants and improve people's quality of life.
slides.note: Scarce means limited in quantity, not unavailable.

slides.title: Opportunity Cost
slides.kicker: Choose one, wave goodbye to the other
bullets: When one alternative is chosen, the other options are given up.
The value of what is given up is known as the opportunity cost.
A farmer with limited land, water and labour must decide how much barley and how much wheat to grow.

items: Value of wheat lost is opportunity cost

slides.note: Even a free-looking choice costs your next best option.

slides.title: The Farmer's Combinations
slides.kicker: One plot of land, five possible farms
bullets: With the same land the farmer can grow 100 kg wheat and no barley, 100 kg barley and no wheat, or a mix between.
The book's table shows combinations A to E: 0 and 100, 25 and 90, 50 and 70, 75 and 40, 100 and 0 kg.
More barley always means less wheat, because land, water and labour are fixed.
slides.note: Trace each point aloud: A, B, C, D, E.

slides.title: Reading the PPC
slides.kicker: A downward slope full of trade-offs
bullets: Plotting the combinations gives a downward sloping curve called the Production Possibility Curve (PPC).
The PPC shows the trade-off between barley and wheat produced with the given resources.
As the farmer moves from A to E, more barley and less wheat is produced; the wheat sacrificed is the opportunity cost of barley.
slides.note: PPC definition: different combinations of goods produced using all available resources.

slides.title: Efficiency on the Curve
slides.kicker: Maximum output, zero wastage
bullets: All points on the PPC show the maximum output that can be produced through efficient use of resources by avoiding wastage.
Producing on the curve means land, water and labour are fully and smartly used.
This helps in better planning and decision-making by enterprises and governments.
slides.note: Curve par rehna means zero wastage. Stay on the curve!

slides.title: Three Key Questions
slides.kicker: What, how and for whom to produce
bullets: Every economy must decide what and how much will be produced, how it will be produced, and who will get to use it and at what prices.
The answers depend on how the resources used to produce goods and services are organised, and who controls the decision-making.
An economy is the state of a country or region in production and consumption of goods and services, and the flow of money.

items: What and how much to produce?
Who gets it, and at what price?

slides.note: Same three questions, different systems, different answers.

slides.title: What Is an Economic System?
slides.kicker: The rulebook for production and distribution
bullets: An economic system defines the mechanisms for the production, consumption and distribution of goods, services and resources of a country.
The book explains three kinds of economic systems: planned, market and mixed.
Each system answers the three key questions differently, based on who owns and controls resources.
slides.note: Mixed economy enters through the book's own activity questions.

slides.title: Inside a Planned Economy
slides.kicker: The government holds the steering wheel
bullets: A central planning authority of the government, such as a planning commission, makes all major economic decisions in the market.
It decides what and how much will be produced, how, and who will get to use them and at what prices.
The government owns most resources and sectors like land, factories, banks and transport; private ownership is limited.
slides.note: Targets first, market demand later, if at all.

slides.title: Planned Economy Trade-offs
slides.kicker: Order and control, but less spark
bullets: Enterprises usually follow the central authority's targets rather than market demand.
Strict permits and licenses prevent a large number of enterprises from operating, which restricts competition among private enterprises.
With little competition there is little motivation to improve quality or innovate. Examples: the former Soviet Union, North Korea and Cuba.
slides.note: Soviet Union, North Korea, Cuba: remember these three.

slides.title: Inside a Market Economy
slides.kicker: Demand and supply take the lead
bullets: What, how and how much to produce are addressed mainly by the forces of demand and supply, with little government intervention.
Ownership of factories, shops, land and other resources largely rests with individuals and private companies.
The government acts like a referee in a football match: it ensures safety and law and order, and does not control prices or production.
slides.note: USA, Japan and Hong Kong are the book's examples.

slides.title: Competition Powers Markets
slides.kicker: Many sellers, better quality, lower prices
bullets: Many producers offer similar products, which encourages better quality, lower prices and innovation in production.
Even in market economies governments play an important role, such as providing public goods and physical infrastructure.
Pure economic systems rarely exist in reality, so real countries blend market freedom with government guidance.
slides.note: Referee bhi zaroori hai. Markets need rules too.

slides.title: Wants, Production, Environment
slides.kicker: More wants, more extraction, more pressure
bullets: The book asks why people's wants keep changing over time and how that affects production in an economy.
It also asks why all our wants cannot be satisfied, since resources stay limited while wants grow.
The constant desire for more creates pressure on the environment, so fulfilment of wants and extraction of resources must be balanced.
slides.note: Balancing wants and extraction is the real challenge.

slides.title: Scarce but Wasted
slides.kicker: Find the leak in your region
bullets: Activity: think of a resource in your region that is scarce but used wastefully.
Then suggest how it could be managed better, through planning and avoiding wastage.
This is exactly what efficient use of resources means on the Production Possibility Curve.
slides.note: Water in summer? Electricity? Start observing.

slides.title: Freedom, Innovation, Reality
slides.kicker: Which system would you pick?
bullets: The book asks which economic system, market, planned or mixed, gives people the most freedom.
It also asks which system is best suited for promoting innovation, and why.
Pure economic systems rarely exist in reality; a mixed economy is often considered a more practical and effective approach.
slides.note: Real countries usually blend both, the mixed way.

slides.title: The 100 Rupee Choice
slides.kicker: Notebook now or tennis racket later?
bullets: A student has ₹100 and must choose between buying a notebook or saving the money for buying a tennis racket later.
Choosing the notebook means giving up the racket for now, and saving for the racket means giving up the notebook.
The book's own options name this concept: opportunity cost, the value of what is given up.
slides.note: Same logic scales from pocket money to national budgets.

slides.title: Decisions Need Data
slides.kicker: Opportunity cost plus evidence, please
bullets: Understanding opportunity cost improves the quality of economic decision-making by making trade-offs visible.
The book asks: can effective economic decisions be made without reliable data? You must support your answer with an example.
It also asks how a country's present economic choices can shape its long-term future, and why future consequences matter today.
slides.note: No data, no direction. Decisions drift.

slides.title: Economics in the News
slides.kicker: Be a production-decision detective
bullets: Activity: find a news article about a product or commodity such as vegetables, fruits, fuel or electronics.
Look for producers or companies deciding how much to produce or supply.
Write two or three sentences explaining the example and why the production decision was made.
slides.note: Yesterday's newspaper is today's economics case study.

quiz.q: Which of these is a need, not a want?
quiz.why: The book lists food, water and shelter as needs; gadgets, vacations and upgrades are wants.

quiz.q: According to the book, a market can be...
options: Only an app on the internet
Physical or virtual, even on the internet
quiz.why: A market is where buying and selling happens; it could be physical or virtual on the internet.

quiz.q: Which of these is a human-made resource?
quiz.why: Resources can be natural like water and coal, or human-made like capital and technology.

quiz.q: A factory uses its steel for medical equipment. What does it give up?
options: Other uses like aircraft or refrigerators
quiz.why: The book shows alternative uses of steel; choosing one means the other options are given up.

quiz.q: The four factors of production are...
quiz.why: The book lists land, labour, capital and technology as the factors of production.

quiz.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as...
options: The value of what is given up when one alternative is chosen
The price of a good in the market
The profit earned by an enterprise
quiz.why: When one alternative is chosen, the value of what is given up is the opportunity cost.

quiz.q: In the farmer's table, moving from combination B to combination C means...
options: Barley rises 25 kg, wheat falls 20 kg
quiz.why: B is 25 kg barley with 90 kg wheat; C is 50 kg barley with 70 kg wheat.

quiz.q: Why does the PPC slope downward as the farmer moves from A to E?
options: Wheat output rises along with barley
Producing more barley forces some wheat to be sacrificed
quiz.why: To grow more barley some wheat must be sacrificed; that trade-off is the opportunity cost.

quiz.q: In a planned economy, all major economic decisions are made by...
options: The forces of demand and supply
A central planning authority of the government
quiz.why: A central planning authority, such as a planning commission, makes all major economic decisions.

quiz.q: Which pair of planned economies appears in the book?
options: Former Soviet Union and North Korea
quiz.why: The book's planned economy examples are the former Soviet Union, North Korea and Cuba.

quiz.q: In a market economy, the government acts like...
options: A referee in a football match
quiz.why: It ensures safety and law and order, and does not control prices or production.

quiz.q: Why is there little motivation to innovate in a planned economy?
options: Strict permits, targets and low competition reduce the push to improve
Consumers refuse to buy new products
Demand and supply change too quickly
quiz.why: Limited private ownership and heavy regulation restrict competition, so quality and innovation suffer.

quiz.q: A student with ₹100 chooses between a notebook and saving for a tennis racket. Which concept explains this?
quiz.why: This is the book's own question; the value of the forgone choice is the opportunity cost.

quiz.q: The chapter's activities say the constant desire for more creates pressure on...
options: The environment through extraction of resources
quiz.why: Fulfilment of unlimited wants increases extraction of resources, pressing on the environment.

quiz.q: Which system does the book suggest is often the most practical in the real world?
quiz.why: Pure economic systems rarely exist; a mixed economy is often more practical and effective.

quiz.q: Why must a country's present economic choices consider future consequences?
options: Because today's choices shape the country's long-term future
quiz.why: The book asks how present economic choices shape the long-term future, so consequences must be weighed.

examples.title: Opportunity cost on the farmer's land
examples.problem: A farmer has one piece of land and can grow barley or wheat. From the book's table, combination C is 50 kg barley with 70 kg wheat, and combination D is 75 kg barley with 40 kg wheat. If the farmer moves from C to D, what extra barley is gained and what is the opportunity cost?
steps: Read combination C from the table: 50 kg barley and 70 kg wheat.
Read combination D: 75 kg barley and 40 kg wheat.
Extra barley gained: 75 minus 50 equals 25 kg.
The value of what is given up, here 30 kg of wheat, is the opportunity cost of the extra barley.
examples.answer: Moving from C to D gains 25 kg of barley at an opportunity cost of 30 kg of wheat.

examples.title: Sorting needs from wants
examples.problem: This month a family bought food grains, paid for water and shelter, and also bought a new gadget and planned a vacation. Using the chapter's definitions, classify each item as a need or a want.
steps: Recall the definition: needs are essentials like food, water and shelter.
Sort the essentials: food grains, water and shelter are needs.
Recall that wants are items like gadgets, vacations or luxury items.
Sort the extras: the new gadget and the vacation are wants.
Remember the book's warning: wants are unlimited and keep changing, like upgrading from a bicycle to a motorbike to a car, while resources to satisfy them are limited.
examples.answer: Needs: food grains, water and shelter. Wants: the gadget and the vacation. Limited resources force the family to choose between them.

examples.title: The 100 rupee decision
examples.problem: A student has ₹100 and must choose between buying a notebook now or saving the money for buying a tennis racket later. Which economic concept best explains this situation, and what exactly is the opportunity cost if the notebook is bought?
steps: Identify the two alternatives: the notebook today or the tennis racket later.
Note that the same ₹100 cannot buy both, so one must be given up.
If the notebook is bought, the forgone alternative is the tennis racket.
Apply the definition: the value of what is given up is the opportunity cost.
Match with the book's own options: demand, opportunity cost, production, inflation. The correct concept is opportunity cost.
examples.answer: The concept is opportunity cost, and if the notebook is bought, its opportunity cost is the tennis racket given up.

flowchart.title: How choice becomes an economic system

steps.label: Wants are unlimited
steps.detail: Preferences range from food and shelter to gadgets, vacations and a car.

steps.label: Resources are limited
steps.detail: Natural and human-made resources exist in limited quantity with alternative uses.

steps.label: Choices must be made
steps.detail: Households, enterprises and governments pick how to use scarce resources.

steps.label: Opportunity cost appears
steps.detail: The value of the next best option given up is the cost of choosing.

steps.label: Map the PPC
steps.detail: Combinations like the farmer's barley and wheat trace a downward curve.

steps.label: Stay efficient
steps.detail: Points on the curve give maximum output by avoiding wastage.

steps.label: Choose a system
steps.detail: Planned, market or mixed arrangements answer what, how and for whom.

steps.label: System shapes results
steps.detail: Ownership and control decide prices, competition, quality and innovation.
